items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — the call opened 'I moving company, this is Chris. How can I help you?' and went straight to data collection. On a 14-minute three-scenario interstate quote, setting the roadmap ('I'll get your details, then walk you through pricing — about 10-15 minutes') was exactly what this call needed and never happened.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Never checked availability for the move date. He identified Sept 26 as a 'Saturday' and moved on — never said whether Einstein has crews and two trucks open that day, on a 99%-certain date the customer volunteered in her first sentence.
Chris never once used the customer's name. She used his four times ('sounds perfect Chris, thank you so much'); he never said 'Rana' at all — well short of the 3+ standard.

No stairs/floors probe. He learned from the property record 'it looks like that's a two story house' but never asked about stair counts, and never flagged that the unknown Houston destination could be a third-floor walk-up apartment — a material time and cost variable on a job he was about to quote at $11K.

No access-concerns probe at all — no elevator, parking, gate, or HOA/COI questions. The customer said outright they were 'shopping around for an apartment or a home' in Houston, which is the single loudest cue on this call to pre-frame apartment access as a variable.
Never asked about storage. Destination was TBD until Sept 12 with a Sept 26 move — the classic setup for a storage stop or a hold — and it was never raised.

Never asked how many boxes the customer has, never asked about additional rooms (garage, attic, patio, storage unit) in a 3,300 sq ft four-bedroom home, and never asked about specialty items (piano, safe, gun safe, antiques) before quoting a multi-day interstate job.
No special-considerations probe — long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns, driveway access.

Never asked the moving-stressor question. She handed him the opening twice: 'we're moving for work and so work is giving us a ten K' and 'coming back to pack sounds a little challenging right now.' He answered the cost math but never named the stress or the budget cap out loud.
No 'pricing is super simple' framing. The pricing block opened 'our price is based in hourly rates' and immediately branched into two-day versus three-day overnight-hotel logistics.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — the biggest single miss. This is a 240-260 mile interstate move with an overnight truck hold, exactly the job where a customer's unspoken fear is 'what happens to my stuff between Grand Prairie and Houston,' and the $2,000 coverage was never said.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch — no credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees. He got partway there with 'there's no deposit and there's actually no fee to cancel or reschedule,' but never ran the differentiator, which matters more than usual here because this quote does carry a $1,560-per-truck transportation fee.

Clock explanation incomplete: '15 minute increments' landed, but he never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens. On a job where the customer is paying $444/hour, when the meter starts is not a detail.

The stated total doesn't reconcile with his own inputs. He gave 19 hours at four movers plus a $3,120 transportation fee plus ~$300 materials, which is roughly $11,856 — but said '$11,096.' Along the way the customer heard him say '10:10 to fifteen K' and had to ask 'So you said 10:10 to fifteen K?' The number he actually left her with does not match his own math, and it was delivered verbally rather than confirmed in writing on the call.
Walk distance and traffic never mentioned as variables, on a four-hour drive that ends inside Houston.

The Save Your Ass prep speech never happened. He landed the cost/time principle — 'definitely the less there is to do, since most of our pricing is based around time' — but there were no consolidation examples (kids' toys, garden tools, loose items in drawers, photos off walls) and no 'take a carload' tip, on a customer who was actively deciding how much to pack herself. This was the highest-value 60 seconds available on this call and it was skipped.

No booking attempt of any kind. The customer closed with 'I'm gonna call like two to three other companies and just ask for quotes' and Chris replied 'Alright, sounds good.' No hold offer, no 'no deposit so let's put Sept 26 on the schedule now and you can cancel free if plans change' — despite having just told her cancellation is free, which is the perfect setup for a risk-free close.

No BOLDED-details framing for the email and no 'reply with any corrections' — notable because the destination address is still unknown and the email is carrying three different quotes, so written verification is doing real work here.
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' as a check, and never gave office hours.
Insurance never explained at all — no No Worries, no 60¢/lb baseline.
No Ecobox or Sparefoot mention despite an active boxes-and-materials conversation and a TBD destination that could need storage.
top_strength: Chris knows the product cold and was genuinely honest about cost. When the customer asked for three separate scenarios — full pack, kitchen-only hybrid, and load-only — he took all three on without flinching: 'We definitely do the kitchen is generally the most time intensive but obviously if we're not packing all the closets... that would reduce the cost and time needed to complete it.' He explained the crew and truck math from real capacity ('we have 26 foot box trucks... roughly the equivalent of a 1700-1800 square foot home pretty standardly furnished, so anything upwards of 3000 would need a two truck crew'), gave a defensible time range ('a typical move for a house this size takes anywhere from seven to nine hours without packing, plus a three and a half to four hour drive'), and volunteered the overnight structure that saves the customer money rather than the one that makes Einstein more: 'they would pack and load everything onto our trucks and keep it on our trucks overnight at our office, you're not charged an overnight fee.' He also billed materials honestly and unprompted — 'say we bring seventy boxes and only end up having used forty of them, you just charge for those forty boxes' — and closed with a clean no-risk frame: 'there's no deposit need to book it... and there's actually no fee to cancel or reschedule.' Product mastery is not the gap on this call.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: give the number first, then the logistics. The customer asked for a rough estimate three separate times — 'are you able to give me somewhat of an estimate?', then 'A little bit but I guess I'm still kinda just lost,' then 'could you give me like a rough number' — and each time Chris went back into overnight-fee and crew-routing detail before producing a figure. What he should have said the first time she asked: 'Rana, here's the short version — full pack is about eleven thousand, kitchen-only is about X, and load-only is about Y, all in. Now let me show you where those numbers come from.' Headline, then the math. He had the answer the whole time; he buried it, and a customer who was ready to buy left the call saying she was going to call two or three competitors. Second priority, and it's the same 90 seconds: he never attempted the booking. He had a 99%-certain Sept 26 Saturday date, a work-funded $10K budget, and he had just told her cancellation and rescheduling are free — that is a risk-free close sitting on the table. The line was 'Since there's no deposit and no cancel fee, let me put Saturday the 26th on the schedule right now so you don't lose the date while you're shopping — if Houston falls through you cancel free.' Third: this is a 240-mile interstate move with an overnight truck hold and No Worries Damage Coverage was never mentioned once. Every long-haul quote should carry it: 'And because your stuff is on our truck overnight, our No Worries coverage is up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage.' Business items to fix today: (1) the quoted total does not reconcile — 19 hours at $444 plus $3,120 transport plus ~$300 materials is about $11,856, not the '$11,096' he stated, and the customer separately heard 'ten to fifteen K'; the emailed three-option breakdown must be checked line by line before it goes out or this becomes a pricing dispute. (2) The Houston destination is unknown until Sept 12, and no apartment-access, stairs, elevator, or COI variables were pre-framed — if she lands in a mid-rise, the quote he emailed is already wrong. Add one line to the email: 'These estimates assume ground-floor or short-carry access at the destination; send me the address when you have it and I'll confirm.' (3) He committed to sending three quotes with a specific hour estimate for each; that email is now the whole deal and needs to go out before she calls the competitors.
phone_presence_notes: Knowledgeable, patient and never defensive when asked the same question three times ('Oh, yeah, for sure. I'm just kind of going over the pricing'), and the customer ended genuinely positive — but the call was monologue-heavy with almost no acknowledgment of what she said, zero use of her name across 14 minutes, and no empathy marker when she volunteered that this was a work relocation on a $10K cap.
audio_review_reason: Two reasons. The dollar figures in this transcript are badly mangled by ASR ('$10.0101 billion', '$250.50 to $350', '44 man team'), so the quote-accuracy deduction needs audio to confirm what he actually said versus what the customer heard. And the central finding — that his explanation ran long and lost the customer twice — is a pace-and-clarity judgment that should be verified by ear before it's coached.
